Render a landscape as an interactive 3D terrain map

Source: R/ls_plot_terrain.R
ls_plot_terrain.Rd

Bins a set of 2D co-ordinates onto a fine grid and renders them as a 3D terrain, in the style of a population density map. Each bin becomes a column whose height follows the number of documents nearby, so dense regions rise as peaks and sparse regions sit as low plains. When a grouping variable is supplied, each column is coloured by the groups that occupy it and every group gets a label anchored to its highest peak.

The output is a single self-contained HTML file. It is drawn with WebGL in the browser, so it needs no JavaScript libraries and works offline (fonts fall back to system fonts when there is no internet connection).

Usage

ls_plot_terrain(
  df,
  x_var = V1,
  y_var = V2,
  group_var = NULL,
  text_var = NULL,
  sample_by = NULL,
  bins = NULL,
  bandwidth = 1.6,
  roughness = 0.25,
  height_scale = c("relief", "sqrt", "linear", "log"),
  spread = 0.35,
  compress_outliers = TRUE,
  height_by = c("auto", "count", "density"),
  colour_by = c("auto", "group", "enrichment"),
  place_names = TRUE,
  exaggeration = 1,
  land_threshold = 0.2,
  colours = NULL,
  labels = NULL,
  title = NULL,
  subtitle = NULL,
  caption = NULL,
  theme = c("paper", "dark"),
  file = NULL,
  open = NULL
)

Arguments

df

Data frame or tibble, one row per document.

x_var, y_var

Variables holding the x and y co-ordinates.

group_var

Optional grouping variable (for example a cluster or topic) used to colour and label the terrain.

text_var

Optional text variable. One example document per bin is shown in the hover tooltip.

sample_by

Optional expression that chooses which documents are shown as examples in the hover tooltip and the place panels. It is evaluated using the columns of df, as in dplyr::filter() or dplyr::arrange(). A logical result acts as a filter, so only rows where it is TRUE are shown, for example label == "clean". A numeric result ranks the rows from highest to lowest, for example relevance. Use -relevance to rank from lowest to highest. To filter and rank at once, give NA to the rows you want left out, for example ifelse(label == "clean", relevance, NA). A date cannot be used to rank directly: write as.numeric(date) to rank by it, or a comparison such as date >= "2024-01-01" to filter by it. Rows where the result is NA are never shown, and ties are broken at random. It changes only which text is shown, not the heights or colours of the map, so a strict filter can leave many columns with no example to show on hover.

bins

Number of bins along the longer axis. Higher values give finer detail. By default it grows with the number of rows, from 200 up to 420.

bandwidth

Smoothing applied to the counts, in bins. Larger values give rounder hills.

roughness

Between 0 and 1. How much fine-grained texture from the raw counts is mixed into the smoothed surface.

height_scale

How density maps onto height. "relief" (default) sets a sea level so sparse ground stays flat and dense regions rise steeply, with the very tallest peaks softened so one large cluster does not flatten the rest. "linear", "sqrt" and "log" are plain transforms of the density, each lifting the low ground more than the last.

spread

How far to push groups apart, as a fraction of the distance between each group's centre and the overall centre. Gives clusters room to breathe. Groups that are mixed together are hardly moved. Set to 0 to keep the original co-ordinates.

compress_outliers

Pull far-flung points and groups in towards the main landmass so that it fills the view. Groups are moved whole, so their shape is kept.

height_by

"count" makes the peak of each group's mountain proportional to its number of documents, so heights compare topic sizes. "density" uses local density, so tight clusters rise higher than loose ones of the same size. "auto" (default) uses "count" when groups occupy their own regions, and "density" otherwise.

colour_by

"group" colours each bin by the groups in it. "enrichment" colours each bin by the group that is most over-represented there compared with its overall share, and leaves bins close to the average neutral. This suits variables such as sentiment that are spread across the whole map. "auto" (default) picks "enrichment" when the groups are heavily mixed.

place_names

When text_var is supplied, name regions of the map by their most distinctive words. Finer place names appear as you zoom in, and clicking a place opens a panel with its keywords and example documents.

exaggeration

Multiplier for the height of the peaks.

land_threshold

Controls how far the base plate extends around the points. Lower values give a larger landmass and more islands around outlying points.

colours

Optional vector of colours for the groups. Can be named by group level.

labels

Optional named character vector to rename group labels, for example c("1" = "Browser privacy").

title, subtitle, caption

Text for the poster-style header and footer. subtitle sits in small capitals above the title.

theme

"paper" (light) or "dark".

file

Path to write the HTML to. If NULL a temporary file is used.

open

By default (NULL) the map is returned visibly, so it opens when printed at the console and is embedded when used in R Markdown, Quarto or a pkgdown article. TRUE opens it straight away and FALSE only writes the file; both return the result invisibly.

Value

An object of class ls_terrain holding the file path. Printing it opens the map.

Details

In the browser you can drag to rotate, shift-drag (or right-drag) to pan and scroll to zoom. Hovering over a column shows the documents and groups beneath it. Clicking a group in the legend isolates it. Shift-click adds groups to the selection. The toolbar can flatten the map to a 2D view, rotate it slowly and download a high-resolution PNG.

Only the binned summary is written to the file, so large data sets (millions of rows) produce files of roughly the same size as small ones. The exception is text_var, which stores one example document per bin.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
ls_example %>%
  ls_plot_terrain(V1, V2, group_var = cluster, text_var = text,
                  title = "Browser Conversation", subtitle = "Landscape of")

# A single-colour density map
ls_example %>% ls_plot_terrain(V1, V2, title = "Density")
} # }
